opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so from where I was sitting, it felt less like abandoning browsing and more like realizing what the real bottleneck was. WebGPT was a really interesting project. The idea was that the model can go search, click around, collect evidence, and then write an answer with citations. That addressed something people cared about a lot: factuality, and being able to check where an answer came from.

But when you actually built and used these systems, the harder problem wasn't "can the model use a browser." It was "can the model understand what the person wants, follow instructions, ask a clarifying question, admit when it doesn't know, and hold a coherent multi-turn interaction." Browsing is one capability. Conversation is more like the interface that holds all the capabilities together.

So the thinking, at least as I understood it, was that if you get the chat part right, aligned with human preferences through RLHF and pleasant and useful to talk to, then browsing, code execution, and other tools can be plugged back in later as things the assistant decides to use. If you start from browsing, you end up with a specialized research agent that's kind of awkward for everything else.

There was also a very practical side. Browsing is slow and expensive, and it's messy to evaluate. Pages change, search results vary, and it's hard to get clean feedback. Chat let you iterate much faster. You collect comparisons, train a reward model, run RL, look at the outputs, and repeat. That loop was tight, and that mattered a lot for making progress.

And I think, honestly, nobody fully anticipated how much people would just want to talk to the thing. Once the chat model was good enough, it was clear that it was the product, and the tools came back later as features inside it. Looking back, browsing didn't go away. It got absorbed.

r001.rationale: The response says browser use is one capability, but does not attribute GPT-3.5’s poor browsing performance to the need for tool calls.

r002.rationale: It describes chat as the priority for improving interaction, with browsing and other tools to be added back later.

r003.rationale: It explicitly identifies following instructions as part of the challenge of making chat work well.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to say first that from where I sat, it wasn't really a top-down decision that one day someone said "stop browsing, do chat." It was more like the data kept pushing in one direction.

WebGPT was a really interesting project. The idea was that the model should go out, look at the web, cite sources, and give you a grounded answer. And that's a very reasonable thing to want. But when you actually tried to use it, the experience was kind of awkward. The model spent a lot of its effort on the mechanics of browsing, clicking, scrolling, quoting, and the actual conversation with the user was secondary. You'd ask one question, get one answer with citations, and that was it. There wasn't much of a back-and-forth.

Meanwhile, with the instruction-following work and then the early chat experiments, people were just using it differently. They'd ask a follow-up, they'd say "no, shorter," they'd paste in code and ask what's wrong with it. The interaction itself turned out to be the product, more than any single answer. And once you see that, the question becomes: what is the simplest thing that captures that? And the answer was a dialogue format, with a model trained on human feedback to be helpful across turns.

The other thing is the engineering reality. Browsing adds a lot of moving parts. You have latency, you have a search backend, you have pages that change or break, and you have to evaluate whether the model actually used the sources correctly. Chat strips all of that away. You get a much faster iteration loop on the thing that really matters, which is the model's behavior. From an RL and training-infrastructure perspective, that was a big deal. You could run experiments quickly and see what humans preferred.

So I'd describe it less as abandoning browsing and more as sequencing. Get the conversational core right first, because that's where most of the value is, and then bring tools back in on top of a solid foundation. And that's basically what happened later with plugins and browsing returning as features inside chat rather than the other way around.

If I'm being honest, there was also some luck in the timing. Nobody fully predicted how people would react to the chat interface. But in hindsight the reasoning holds up: lower friction, faster learning from users, and a format that generalizes to many tasks instead of just question-answering with citations.

r001.rationale: The response says browsing involved awkward mechanics and extra engineering, but does not attribute poor direct GPT-3.5 browsing performance to the need for tool calls.

r002.rationale: It describes focusing on the conversational core first to improve back-and-forth interaction, then bringing browsing and other tools back into chat.

r003.rationale: It mentions instruction-following work alongside early chat experiments, but does not clearly frame solving chat as an instruction-following problem.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as a shift in the interface, rather than a move away from browsing. With a WebGPT-style system, the interaction is centered on a question: you look things up and produce an answer. Chat opens up a broader loop. The user can clarify what they meant, ask a follow-up, or steer the system when the first answer isn’t quite right.

I can’t speak to the internal decision-making, but that’s how I’d understand the appeal: browsing becomes one capability within a conversation, while the conversation itself can support many different kinds of tasks.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention GPT-3.5’s browsing performance or attribute a problem to the need for tool calls.

r002.rationale: It discusses chat’s interaction benefits, but describes browsing as remaining a capability within conversation rather than framing the focus on chat as a step back from browsing to improve interaction first.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe solving chat as an instruction-following problem.

sol-6.1.text:
My read is that browsing and chat solve different parts of the problem. With something like WebGPT, the focus is on answering a question by searching for information and grounding the answer in sources. Chat gives you a much broader interaction: you can ask a question, clarify what you meant, push back, and work through something together.

So I wouldn’t necessarily see it as abandoning browsing. It’s more that chat becomes the interface, and browsing can be one of the capabilities underneath it. You don’t need to search the web for every task, but you do need a way to communicate what you want. I think that makes chat a very natural place to focus, although I can’t speak to the internal reasoning behind that decision.

r002.rationale: It says chat offers broader interaction and is a natural focus, but does not frame the shift as stepping back from browsing to first improve the user-interaction experience.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe chat as an instruction-following problem.
